title: The month of Maghar
hook: in Maghar lovely are those who sit with the Beloved (Barah Maha, ang 135)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katak, and your line: katak: blame no one. Did you catch an alibi as it formed? This week walked through six months: Jeth's bowing, Asarh's heat, Sawan's blossom, Bhadon's doubt, Assu's question, Katak's honesty. Today, the week ends sitting down together. Day five hundred seventy-four.

Some good hours happen with nothing going on. A kitchen late at night, two people with tea, the dishes not done. A hospital waiting room where a friend just sits beside you and doesn't try to say anything wise. A grandparent on a bench, holding a small hand, watching pigeons. Nobody would put these moments on a highlight reel. But they can be the ones that stay. Maghar, roughly mid-November to mid-December, is when the Punjabi cold starts to come in, and people pull their chairs closer. Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza is about exactly that: sitting with.
screen: `TEA AT A LATE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `A FRIEND IN THE WAITING ROOM.` → `MAGHAR: SITTING WITH.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Maghar, lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the Lord. Sohandee-aa, lovely, shining. And baithrree-aah, those who sit. That's all they're doing. They aren't climbing, earning or proving. They're seated beside the One they love, and the stanza says their beauty can't even be counted. Then it adds the other side. Those who don't sit in the company of the holy, it says, stay alone. Their pain doesn't leave them, and they fall into death's grip. There's a whole Sikh practice inside that one picture. Think of the diwan hall of a gurdwara. People take off their shoes, cover their heads, bow, and then sit on the floor, together, at the same level. Nobody has a better chair. They sit while the hymns are sung, sometimes for a long time, sometimes saying nothing at all. That's sangat, the holy company, and in the Barah Maha it's where the bride finds the Beloved's presence. Look back at the week and you can see the road. In Jeth she bowed. In Asarh she learned to keep Him near in the heat. In Sawan she blossomed, in Bhadon she doubted, in Assu she longed and asked how. In Katak she stopped blaming. And now, in Maghar, she simply sits. The stanza ends: in Maghar, those who worship the Lord are not born again into the round of coming and going. The long journey of the months arrives somewhere very still. Lovely are the ones who sit.
screen: `SOHANDEE-AA: LOVELY ARE THOSE WHO SIT.` · `APART FROM THE HOLY, WE STAY ALONE.` · `SANGAT: SEATED ON ONE FLOOR.` · `THE WEEK'S ROAD ARRIVES IN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `MAGHAR: SIT TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone you love. If someone you love is near, sit beside them now, no phone, no agenda, just two people in the same room. If no one is near, bring one person to mind and sit as if they were next to you. Picture their face, their hands, the way they settle into a chair. Don't plan a conversation. Just be with. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the stanza calls the Beloved. The bell holds the time.
Maghar. In the Barah Maha, Maghar is the month of sitting: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, and the holy company is where we sit.
Your line: maghar: sit together. Today, give one person ten minutes of sitting with them and nothing else. Tea counts. A bench counts. Day five hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sit together on the floor of the diwan hall, at one level, to hear kirtan; on the Sangrand of Maghar gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza from the Barah Maha.

myth: in the Maghar stanza, the lovely ones are busy proving their devotion
they're simply seated with the Beloved; sitting is the whole picture.
the stanza says those apart from the holy company stay alone
it says their pain doesn't leave them; the sangat is where the bride finds company.
in a gurdwara's diwan hall, everyone sits on the floor at one level
nobody has a better chair while the hymns are sung.

fork.setup: the long road of the months has brought the bride to Maghar. what does she do there?
options: work harder to deserve the Beloved.
fork.reveal: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the stanza says. after bowing, longing and owning her deeds, she simply sits.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the company, the congregation that sits together to sing and listen.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maghar is a cold month, so the stanza is about weather.
what it means: it's about the beauty of simply sitting with the Beloved, in holy company.
what a scholar hears: the stanza promises that those who worship the Lord in Maghar are not born again, placing the end of the cycle of births in an act as plain as sitting.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Maghar stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed the review's count (it named six months and said seven); the teach no longer calls the stanza's warning 'tender, not harsh' and now keeps its line about falling into death's power; cut 'the best hours' and 'ask people... it's often these'.

Paraphrase of the Maghar stanza (manghir maahi sohandee-aa har pir sang baithrree-aah ... saadhoo sang na baisnee se rahan ikelee-aah ... manghir prabh aaraadhanaa bahurh na janmarree-aah): please confirm wording and Ang 135.
Week look-back names days 568–573 (Jeth, Asarh, Sawan, Bhadon, Assu, Katak); this writer did not see days 568–571's finished scripts.
